newsitem.title: UK: London dealers doubt rerun of 1992 election buzz.
newsitem.headline: London dealers doubt rerun of 1992 election buzz.

text.p: Financial houses in the City of London plan to provide only skeleton cover in the early hours of Friday as the results of the British election roll in, analysts said on Tuesday.

The camp beds, takeaway pizzas and adrenalin that pumped through London's stock, bond and foreign exchange dealing rooms in the last two elections will be notably absent, said traders, as most city folk opt to stay home.
"Most people will be at home watching the results come in on TV," said John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International. "In market terms, it's a bit of a non-event."

Opinion polls which showed the Labour and Conservative Parties neck-in-neck in the 1992 election had trading rooms braced for a busy night. A surprise victory for the Conservatives sent markets into a spin.

Gilts rose around three points, sterling rallied nearly three pfennigs against the mark and the stock market closed more than five percent higher. The Bank of England even sold 1.6 billion sterling of gilts in the middle of the night, an unprecedented move.
But this time round, gilts traders are more likely to be huddled up in bed than around their dealing screens, although most do plan to make an early start on Friday.

"There is the potential for some enormous last minute surprises this time, but given the consistency of the polls, no-one is expecting any stunners on the night," said Shepperd."People will be happy to go to bed and assess things in the morning."
Opinion polls have unfailingly predicted a win for the opposition Labour party on May 1.
Ian Amstad, senior economist at Bankers Trust here, said he was anticipating little overnight demand from clients for gilts.

"There won't be many people spinning the dice on this outcome," he said. "There may be an element of buy on the rumour, sell on the fact, so there may be some profit taking in sterling assets...but we're not expecting any violent shenanigans."
Richard Hill, head of foreign exchange at Bank of America in London, said he did not expect the kind of hectic trading the market experienced in 1992.
"That's really only going to occur if it looks like a repeat," he said, referring to the Conservatives' unexpected victory.

But Hill said there were still likely to be market participants eager to deal as soon as the results started to come out. "I don't think it's going to be crazy, but we should see some interest certainly."

A number of banks were planning to trade equities for clients through the night, including Merrill Lynch which took over Smith New Court in 1995, one of the brokers which worked overnight during the 1992 election.
Analysts said the only thing that would make telephones and dealers scream, was the prospect of a hung parliament.
"We want to see a clear majority which secures a comfortable five years, enough to marginalise what remains of the loony left," said Kevin Adams, gilts analyst at BZW.
Amstad said one of the main factors putting a lid on the excitement was the fact an anticipated Labour government would likely have broadly similar macroeconomic policies to the ruling Conservatives.

Add to that the fact that markets in continental Europe are on holiday on Thursday, British markets are off on Monday and investors will be bracing for U.S. payrolls on Friday, and trade will likely be subdued, traders said.
One dealer whose brokerage planned all night cover said the main problem was boredom.
"It's not so close and it's the first time we've been in a situation where gilts actually seem happy with a Labour government," he said. "People are getting a bit bored with it all."
